morningLine: J.C. Penney backs away from Coleco’s Adam just as the Christmas computer contest reaches full volume.

lead.headline: Penney Drops Coleco's Adam From Holiday Line
lead.dek: A major retailer’s retreat exposes delivery and reliability doubts around the ambitious all-in-one home computer.
body: Coleco’s bid to turn its video-game success into a home-computer empire suffered a conspicuous holiday setback this week. The New York Times reported November 15 that J.C. Penney had omitted the Adam computer from its holiday line, a damaging absence at the moment families were studying Christmas catalogs and retailers were committing scarce shelf space.

Adam had been promoted as a complete household system rather than a bare computer: 64K of memory, keyboard, Digital Data Pack drive and a daisy-wheel printer in a package advertised near $700. That aggressive bundle promised word processing and home entertainment without the long accessory list attached to many rivals.

The promise collided with the difficult work of shipping reliable machines in quantity. Federal marketing approval had arrived in September and store availability was expected in October, so Penney’s November retreat sharpened questions about whether Coleco could meet the season it had spent the year courting.

The episode lands amid a punishing price war. Commodore and Atari are discounting established machines, IBM’s $669 PCjr has entered the conversation, and software libraries increasingly matter as much as specifications. For Adam, missing one retailer’s holiday line is more than a lost sale: it is a test of confidence in the whole package.

stories.headline: Microsoft Opens a Window on DOS
body: Microsoft’s newly announced Windows environment proposes a graphical layer for MS-DOS computers, bringing menus, a pointing device and multiple on-screen work areas to IBM-compatible hardware. The November 10 unveiling remains fresh news as the trade studies an early prerelease system.

The company’s broad compatibility pitch distinguishes Windows from graphical systems tied to one manufacturer. Bill Gates predicted rapid adoption across IBM-compatible machines, though both the software and the market still face a long road from demonstration to everyday desk.

stories.headline: Video Games Enter Christmas Under a Cloud
body: The cartridge business approaches Christmas carrying excess inventory, retailer caution and the shadow of Atari’s losses. Warner Communications reported a $122.3 million third-quarter after-tax loss in October as Atari’s fortunes collapsed.

Yet computer games are showing where players may go next. Ultima III, Archon and Lode Runner offer deeper strategy, construction and role-playing on programmable machines—experiences that dedicated consoles struggle to match.

stories.headline: Schools Add Ethics to Computer Literacy
body: A November 14 Christian Science Monitor report argues that students need values alongside technical skill. After the widely publicized intrusions by Milwaukee’s 414s, access to networks is no longer being discussed as a purely mechanical lesson.

Teachers and parents now confront a new question: how to encourage curiosity without treating an electronic boundary as imaginary. The debate signals that computer literacy is becoming a civic subject as well as a vocational one.

undergroundDesk.headline: Computer Ethics Enters the Classroom
undergroundDesk.dek: After the 414s, educators argue that access skills must come with a sense of responsibility.
body: The national attention surrounding Milwaukee’s 414s has made unauthorized computer access a subject for classrooms as well as security offices. A November 14 education report says technical instruction alone is not enough.
The emerging lesson is ethical rather than operational: curiosity does not erase ownership, privacy or consequences. Schools are beginning to treat responsible access as part of computer literacy.
